findings.source_passage: Yet are there those who will still do it; notwithstanding the fact that the oil obtained from such subjects is of a very inferior quality, and by no means of the nature of attar-of-rose.
findings.source_locator: paragraph 4, closing sentence of the blasted-whale description
findings.why_it_matters: The 'attar-of-rose' joke is a careful, ironic setup for the ship's name reveal that follows; its absence flattens the comic architecture and loses the narrator's dry voice.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the 'by no means of the nature of attar-of-rose' clause before the Rose-bud name reveal.

findings.source_passage: looking as anxious as gold-hunters... his boat's crew were all in high excitement, eagerly helping their chief
findings.why_it_matters: The simile 'looking as anxious as gold-hunters' is a signature ironic register marker — material greed cloaked in whale-work — present in the source but reduced to a bare phrase in the draft without the 'eagerly helping their chief' elaboration; the fuller image carries critical weight on the chapter's treasure-hunt theme.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore 'eagerly helping their chief' alongside 'gold-hunters' to preserve the full ironic comparison.

findings.source_passage: and this was the romantic name of this aromatic ship
findings.why_it_matters: Melville's pun 'romantic name of this aromatic ship' is verbatim present in the draft, but the full buildup — the green stalk, copper spikes, and bright red folded bulb described in lavish detail — is compressed to near-nothing, stripping the comedic contrast that makes the pun land.
findings.suggested_fix: Expand the figurehead description to include the thorned spikes, painted green stalk, and the symmetrical folded bulb before the 'romantic/aromatic' payoff.

findings.source_passage: when at length his spade struck against the gaunt ribs, it was like turning up old Roman tiles and pottery buried in fat English loam
findings.why_it_matters: The draft reduces this to 'ribs rang like Roman tiles in fat loam,' losing 'gaunt ribs,' 'pottery,' and the full archaeological simile's texture; the compression erases a characteristically Melvillean learned-comic digression.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore 'old Roman tiles and pottery buried in fat English loam' as the complete simile rather than the clipped version.

findings.source_passage: And this, good friends, is ambergris, worth a gold guinea an ounce to any druggist.
findings.why_it_matters: The direct address 'good friends' is a register-defining narrator intrusion typical of Melville's rhetorical style; reduced to bare reportage it loses the confidential aside that distinguishes the chapter's voice.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore 'And this, good friends, is ambergris' with the direct address intact.

summary: No high-severity signature losses; three medium findings (attar-of-rose irony absent, gold-hunters elaboration clipped, figurehead description compressed past its comic function) and two low findings that together represent noticeable but non-fatal voice flattening in this passage.
